## 3. Deviations from Gustafson's linear model

* Largest shortfall below the fitted line: P = 12 (residual -0.867987); largest excess: P = 3 (residual +1.015300).
* **SMT boundary.** Up to P = 8 each worker can own a physical core; efficiency at P = 8 is 0.462883. Beyond it, workers share cores with a hyper-thread sibling; at P = 12 efficiency is 0.314352. Two threads on one core share its FP/vector units, so this compute-bound kernel gains little from SMT: the time per worker rises and S(P) bends below the line.
* **Hybrid cores.** 4 cores report SMT (P-cores) and 4 do not (E-cores). Once the scheduler places workers on E-cores, those workers are slower, and because `pool.map` waits for the slowest worker the whole step runs at E-core speed. This shows up as a jump in the per-worker compute column once P exceeds the number of P-cores.
* **Frequency and thermals.** The per-worker compute time (measured inside each worker, excluding dispatch) grows to 3.068191× the single-worker value at P = 12. A single active core runs at its maximum turbo bin; as more cores are loaded the all-core turbo is lower and the package power/thermal limit (PL1/PL2 on laptops) pulls frequency down further. Gustafson's model assumes each processor is as fast as in the serial run, so this frequency loss is folded into the fitted α.
* **Cache and memory.** Each worker processes blocks of 65,536 doubles (≈ 512 KiB per array), which fit in L2 (2 MiB). The kernel is therefore compute-bound and memory bandwidth is not the main limiter; 8 memory module(s) and the shared L3 (12 MiB) mainly matter for NumPy temporaries.
* **NUMA.** The host has 1 NUMA node(s) and 1 package(s), so there is no remote-memory penalty; all deviation comes from cores, frequency, SMT and OS overhead.
* **Python overhead.** Every step pays a constant dispatch cost (pickling the task, waking workers, collecting results). It does not grow with the work per worker and is the true serial part α in this experiment; it is small because each task runs for about a second.

## 4. Conclusion

The Gustafson model fits with R² = 0.4019809054458666 and α = 0.66907212675887. 1 of 12 measured points lie within two standard errors of the fitted line. The remaining deviations are hardware effects not present in the model: shared cores beyond the physical count, heterogeneous core speeds, and lower all-core clock frequency. On a laptop these act like a serial fraction that grows with P, which is why measured efficiency falls faster than the constant 1 − α predicted by an ideal machine.
